title: One platform, four module applications
body:
## The platform underneath everything

POET Technologies built its investment proposition on a single architectural claim: that the conventional method of connecting optical components — soldering discrete lasers, modulators, and photodetectors onto a printed circuit board, then coupling them to fibre — was a structural obstacle to the power densities and bandwidth requirements hyperscalers would need inside the next generation of AI clusters. The POET Optical Interposer was the company's answer. Rather than stacking optical components vertically on silicon or assembling them in sequence on a board, the interposer offered a passive wafer-level substrate onto which multiple optical elements — lasers, modulators, photodetectors, wavelength filters — could be integrated in a single planar process with minimal optical loss at each junction.

The platform's materials-agnostic architecture was its most structurally distinctive characteristic. Where pure silicon photonics approaches were constrained by silicon's inherent limitations as a light source, and where traditional III-V compound-semiconductor designs carried cost and yield penalties at volume, POET's interposer was designed to host both families of devices — InP DFB lasers, silicon photonic modulators, germanium photodetectors — on the same substrate without forcing the designer to accept the worst trade-offs of either material system. The company described this as a "heterogeneous integration" platform, and it was the core IP around which the entire POET thesis rotated.

That platform was not a product. It was the technology substrate from which four distinct module application areas were being developed as of the snapshot date, none of which had reached commercial volume revenue. Understanding the distinction between the platform and its applications is not a semantic exercise — it is the essential frame for any honest reading of POET's competitive position.

## Four applications, none at volume

**800G optical transceiver modules** represented the nearest-term commercial opportunity in POET's product taxonomy as of FY2025. Built on the Optical Interposer, these modules targeted hyperscaler datacenter interconnect at the 800 gigabit-per-second line rate that had become the dominant deployment standard in large AI cluster builds through 2024 and 2025. At the snapshot date, the 800G programme was in customer qualification — the stage at which potential buyers evaluate a component against their own reliability, thermal, and performance specifications before committing to a volume design win. The [FY2025 20-F filing](https://www.stocktitan.net/sec-filings/POET/20-f-poet-technologies-inc-files-annual-report-foreign-issuer-eeda6513f179.html) disclosed no named customers and no commercial design wins. The qualification pipeline was the asset, not the revenue line.

**1.6T optical transceiver modules** sat one generation further out in the product roadmap, targeting the next step-up in interconnect bandwidth that AI server architectures were expected to require as GPU clusters scaled beyond the configurations supported by 800G. At the snapshot date, the 1.6T programme was in development stage — meaning active engineering work was underway but customer qualification had not begun in any disclosed form. The strategic logic was straightforward: a company that demonstrated the 800G interposer architecture to a hyperscaler's satisfaction was positioned to propose the 1.6T follow-on without starting the relationship from scratch. The 1.6T module was, in this reading, both a product in development and a retention mechanism for whatever 800G relationships POET was cultivating.

**External Light Sources for co-packaged optics** constituted the third application, and the one with the clearest disclosed partnership context. In September 2025, POET announced a collaboration with [Sivers Semiconductors](https://www.poet-technologies.com/news/poet-technologies-and-sivers-semiconductors-collaborate-on-external-light-sources-for-co-packaged-optics-and-next-generation-ai-market) — specifically with the UK-based Sivers Photonics subsidiary — to develop ELS modules combining Sivers' custom high-power InP DFB lasers with POET's Optical Interposer. The ELS application addressed a specific architectural constraint in co-packaged optics deployments: when optical engines are co-packaged directly on the same substrate as a GPU or network switch ASIC, the heat generated by the compute package makes it impractical to site the laser source inside the same thermal envelope. An external light source — a separate module that generates the optical signal and pipes it into the co-packaged engine — became the engineering solution, and it was the application POET was explicitly targeting with the Sivers collaboration.

The Sivers partnership was notable for what it revealed about POET's supply chain positioning as much as for the module itself. Both companies were pre-revenue platform bets aiming at the same emerging hyperscaler procurement cycle. Sivers brought InP laser design capability; POET brought the interposer substrate that could integrate those lasers with the other optical components an ELS requires. The collaboration was a component-level alliance between two upstream suppliers, neither of which had yet demonstrated volume shipments to a named hyperscaler customer as of the snapshot date.

**Other photonic integration applications** formed the fourth category — a deliberately open-ended designation covering co-development engagements with customers that had not been publicly disclosed. The 20-F acknowledged these engagements in general terms without naming counterparties. In practice, this bucket captured the bespoke NRE work that generated essentially all of POET's FY2025 revenue.

## Revenue that tells you where the company actually is

The revenue line was the most useful single indicator of POET's commercial maturity at the snapshot date, and it required no euphemism: the company recorded approximately $1.2 million in total revenue for FY2025, comprising non-recurring engineering fees and small product shipments. The quarterly progression — [$298,434 in Q3 2025](https://www.poet-technologies.com/news/poet-technologies-reports-third-quarter-2025-financial-results) and [$341,202 in Q4 2025](https://www.poet-technologies.com/news/poet-technologies-reports-fourth-quarter-2025-financial-results) — showed modest sequential growth but remained orders of magnitude below what would be required to cover even a single quarter of the company's $18.08 million annual R&D expenditure.

| Period | Revenue (USD) | Nature |
|--------|--------------|--------|
| Q3 2024 | $3,685 | NRE / product |
| Q4 2024 | $29,032 | NRE / product |
| Q2 2025 | $268,469 | NRE / product |
| Q3 2025 | $298,434 | NRE / product |
| Q4 2025 | $341,202 | NRE / product |
| **FY2025 total** | **~$1.2M** | **NRE / product** |

The sequential acceleration from near-zero in 2024 to approximately $1.2 million in FY2025 was real but not commercially meaningful in the conventional sense. It reflected deepening customer engagement — engineering teams willing to pay POET to solve specific integration problems — rather than volume procurement. NRE revenue in photonics is the signal that says a hyperscaler's or OEM's engineering organisation took POET seriously enough to fund a joint development effort; it is not, in itself, evidence that a volume design win followed.

## Singapore, manufacturing, and what the filing does not say

The physical integration of POET's modules happened not in Canada — where the company was incorporated and where its corporate headquarters sat — but in Singapore, through the wholly-owned subsidiary POET Singapore Pte. Ltd. Singapore was a deliberate geographic choice that offered proximity to the broader Southeast Asian semiconductor manufacturing cluster and a degree of insulation from the US-China trade friction that had complicated supply chains for optical components dependent on Chinese fabrication capacity. The 20-F disclosed geopolitical exposure across POET's Asian operations footprint — Singapore, China, and Malaysia were all named as operating geographies in the risk factors section — but specifics of the company's wafer fabrication and OSAT relationships were not publicly disclosed at the snapshot date.

What the filing made clear was the nature of the business model. POET was a design-and-IP company, not a fab-owning operator. The interposer process flow — combining silicon photonics process steps with III-V device attach and photonic packaging — was executed through the Singapore integration line, but the company carried no meaningful capital expenditure line at FY2025 scale. Capital allocation ran through two channels: R&D at $18.08 million for the fiscal year (with an additional $2.22 million in non-cash stock compensation layered on top), and SG&A at $25.08 million (inclusive of $3.89 million in stock compensation and $3.32 million in depreciation and amortisation). There was no third channel. POET was spending money to develop the platform and to maintain the commercial and administrative infrastructure around it — full stop.

## The product taxonomy as investment thesis

Taken together, the four application areas formed a portfolio of options on a single architectural bet. The 800G module was the near-term proof point — the application that could, if a qualification succeeded, generate the first commercially meaningful revenue and validate the Optical Interposer's fitness for hyperscaler supply chains. The 1.6T module was the retention play and the roadmap signal. The ELS collaboration with Sivers was the CPO-specific positioning: POET's explicit claim that the interposer architecture could sit usefully in the upstream supply chain of co-packaged optical engines even if it never became the optical engine itself. The fourth bucket, the undisclosed co-development engagements, was the optionality that the market could not price with any precision.

None of the four generated commercial volume at the snapshot date. All four were being funded by the $313.4 million cash position — itself the product of a $250 million institutional equity raise executed in 2025 by three undisclosed institutional buyers. The platform, in other words, was not yet selling to customers at volume. It was selling to investors the proposition that it would.
